title: The U.S. Is About to Design an AI Regulator. Here’s How to Get It Right. | Council on Foreign Relations
gist: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis proposed a FINRA-style, industry-funded Frontier AI Standards Body on July 14, and three days later Bloomberg reported the White House — with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent involved — is reviewing a proposal built on that template. Former NSA and NIST AI officials argue the institutional form is the easy part, and that five unresolved design questions (independence, national security handling, allied legitimacy, guaranteed model access plus talent, and immature measurement science) will decide whether the resulting certification becomes a globally honored badge for U.S. models or a worthless industry stamp.

insights.claim: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis published a framework on July 14, 2026 calling for a U.S.-led Frontier AI Standards Body modeled on FINRA — an industry-funded self-regulatory organization overseen by the SEC — and three days later Bloomberg reported the White House is reviewing a proposal built on that template, developed with Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent's involvement.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Frontier AI oversight in the U.S. is moving from speculation to an active White House design process on a securities-regulation template — a near-term compliance cost and moat-builder for the largest labs.
insights.locator: Google DeepMind CEO Demis Hassabis published a framework

insights.claim: Under the Google proposal, frontier AI companies would submit models for review up to thirty days before release, with testing for dangerous cyber, biological, and deceptive capabilities, starting voluntarily and later becoming a condition of U.S. deployment.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: A 30-day prerelease review window would add a structural lag to frontier model launch cadence and eventually gate U.S. market access entirely.
insights.quote: frontier AI companies would submit their models for review up to thirty days before release
insights.locator: Under Google’s proposal

insights.claim: The choice of institutional form for an AI regulator was never the hard part — a FINRA-inspired body reporting to the SEC is a reasonable answer to a real coordination problem — but financing, guaranteed system access, and classification of findings remain undefined, and those choices decide whether the body survives its first crisis of confidence.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Watch the financing and access clauses, not the org chart, when the White House proposal surfaces — they determine whether the regime is real oversight or theater.
insights.quote: The good news is that the choice of institutional form was never the hard part
insights.locator: The good news is that the choice of institutional form

insights.claim: Having frontier AI companies fund their own evaluators most closely resembles the issuer-pays credit-rating model that undermined public trust during the 2008 financial crisis.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: If the AI body launches industry-funded, expect its ratings to carry a structural credibility discount — and eventual reform risk — exactly as ratings did post-2008.
insights.quote: The closest analogy to companies funding their own evaluators is the issuer-pays credit-rating model, which undermined public trust during the 2008 financial crisis.
insights.locator: Independence. FINRA-style proposals assume industry funding

insights.claim: FINRA tries to manage conflict of interest by requiring public governors to outnumber industry representatives, yet concerns persist about 'composition drift,' where shifting conflicts among public-sector representatives pull the board away from public-sector priorities.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Board-composition safeguards are a weak guarantee of independence; structural separation of functions is the tell to look for instead.
insights.locator: FINRA addresses this by requiring public governors

insights.claim: Safety and testing specifications for frontier AI should be funded exclusively by neutral, non-industry money, with industry money restricted to building shared testing instrumentation — potentially funded through an engineering body such as MLCommons so results across evaluators are comparable.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: MLCommons-style benchmark infrastructure becomes strategically important plumbing if this design is adopted; comparability of eval results is the bottleneck.
insights.quote: no dollar generated by an AI company should influence the process for determining the standards that will govern those companies
insights.locator: First, separate three functions

insights.claim: No institution, public or private, has done frontier model evaluation at scale, so the evaluation function itself is currently unsolved and should be built by pairing a classified-research institution like RAND with civil-rights expertise from nonprofits such as the Center for Democracy & Technology.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: There is no incumbent evaluator with proven scale capacity — a genuine capability gap and a build-out opportunity for research institutions and eval vendors.
insights.quote: no institution, public or private, has done frontier evaluation at scale; standing up that function is currently unsolved
insights.locator: Meanwhile, no institution, public or private

insights.claim: Any agreement should bind multiyear financial commitments from frontier AI companies to guaranteed model access — including access to internal, non-deployed systems — so neither can be quietly withdrawn.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Access to non-deployed internal models is the sharpest concession labs would have to make; its presence or absence signals how binding the regime really is.
insights.locator: Second, bind funding to access

insights.claim: No FINRA examination has ever produced information that was itself a national security asset, but a frontier AI evaluation body will inevitably produce such findings — a structural break from the securities-regulation analogy being copied.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: The FINRA template imports a governance model that never had to handle classified output; mishandling this is the most likely single point of failure.
insights.quote: No FINRA examination has ever produced information that was itself a national security asset.
insights.locator: National security. No FINRA examination

insights.claim: A body holding prerelease access across every frontier lab becomes one of the world's highest-value espionage targets, and overcorrecting toward secrecy risks the United States learning about dangerous capabilities from an adversary first.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Concentrating prerelease model access in one institution creates a new systemic cyber-risk node worth tracking for security spend and for tail-risk on model leakage.
insights.quote: by holding prerelease access across every frontier lab, the body itself will become one of the world’s highest-value espionage targets
insights.locator: National security. No FINRA examination

insights.claim: Tiered disclosure — unclassified ratings, lab-confidential findings, and classified capability details — must be established on day one, because national-security designations expand when left undefined, and a small cleared intelligence-community group should sharpen test design without the government writing the tests.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: If classification rules are set after the first classified finding, expect the public rating layer to hollow out — which would kill the certification's market value.
insights.quote: design the classified interface before the first classified finding, not after
insights.locator: Third, design the classified interface

insights.claim: Frontier model access today is granted at a company's discretion, under an NDA, and on a release-by-release basis, which means an oversight body without guaranteed access can only evaluate what it is permitted to see.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Discretionary, per-release NDA access is the current status quo — any regime that does not replace it leaves labs with de facto veto over their own audits.
insights.quote: Today, access is granted at a company’s discretion, under a non-disclosure agreement, and on a release-by-release basis.
insights.locator: Access and talent. Independence without guaranteed model access

insights.claim: The scarcest resource for frontier AI oversight is talent able to test frontier capabilities in a scientifically valid way, because that expertise has increasingly consolidated within the private sector.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Public-sector evaluation capacity is talent-constrained, not budget-constrained — a durable advantage for labs in any negotiation over standards.
insights.quote: expertise has increasingly consolidated within the private sector
insights.locator: Access and talent. Independence without guaranteed model access

insights.claim: Frontier evaluation must be built into a profession with stable careers, scholarship-for-service recruitment modeled on the intelligence community's answer to the private-sector pay gap, and conflict rules preventing evaluation roles from becoming a waystation to frontier-lab employment.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Revolving-door dynamics between evaluators and labs are the quiet capture mechanism; conflict rules are a cheap tell for whether the regime has teeth.
insights.quote: conflict rules that make evaluation a profession rather than a waystation to frontier company employment
insights.locator: Fourth, turn evaluation into a profession

insights.claim: There is no settled science of frontier AI assessment — benchmarks saturate, results carry unreported uncertainty, and point-in-time certification fails for systems that change between measurements — so the body should certify processes and continuous-monitoring regimes rather than snapshots, and state plainly that early evaluations carry only provisional confidence.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Any headline claim that a model has been 'certified safe' under the new regime should be discounted heavily in its first years — the measurement science does not support it.
insights.quote: benchmarks saturate, results carry unreported uncertainty, and point-in-time certification fails for systems that change between measurements
insights.locator: Measurement. There is no settled science

insights.claim: Individual assessments can be developed in isolation but no broader accountability ecosystem or set of industry standards exists to translate evaluation findings into practical changes in how frontier systems are deployed.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Evaluation output today has no enforcement transmission channel — the missing link between a finding and a deployment change is where the real regulatory power will sit.
insights.locator: Assessments can be developed in isolation

insights.claim: Allies in Brussels, London, Seoul, and Tokyo will be reluctant to accept an American industry-funded body as an arbiter of international AI standards, and the domestic public will not trust a body that measures only what companies and security agencies fear while jobs, privacy, and inequality go unexamined.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Without allied buy-in, U.S. AI certification does not travel — expect competing EU/UK/Korea/Japan regimes and duplicated compliance cost for labs.
insights.locator: Legitimacy. Allies in Brussels, London, Seoul, and Tokyo

insights.claim: Seats for allied governments and public-interest organizations plus protected funding for rights-based assessments such as privacy and confidentiality should be embedded in the architecture now, because a certification issued by a body excluding the affected public and allied partners will not produce the intended effect.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Embedded allied representation is the cheapest determinant of whether the certification is honored in export markets — a design detail with direct revenue consequences for U.S. labs.
insights.quote: Embedded representation is not a cynical play for political legitimacy. It is a critical investment into converting a technical finding into a trusted imprimatur
insights.locator: Lastly, embed allied governments

insights.claim: A well-built U.S. AI standards body would give American models a badge of quality, reliability, safety, and trust to carry into markets where they compete against cheaper stacks reflecting someone else's standards; built as an industry stamp it becomes a credential few at home or abroad have incentive to honor.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Frames AI regulation as an export-competitiveness instrument versus cheaper foreign model stacks, not just a cost — relevant to how U.S. labs price and market internationally.
insights.quote: Built in the image of an industry stamp, however, it will be a credential few at home or abroad have any incentive to honor.
insights.locator: The FINRA-for-AI moment is real

insights.claim: Industry can fund and staff most of what is missing in frontier AI oversight but cannot supply its own neutral convener, so a coalition of a defense-credible research institution, a civil-society technology organization, a benchmark-engineering body, a measurement science group, and a neutral convener should put a fuller design on the table for the White House.
insights.speaker: Vinh Nguyen
insights.so_what: Signals an organized push to widen the design process beyond Google's proposal — watch for a counter-blueprint coalition emerging before the White House decides.
insights.quote: What it cannot do—as leaders across finance, energy, and the labs themselves acknowledge behind closed doors—is to supply its own neutral convener.
insights.locator: Industry can fund and staff most of what is missing
